Checiny Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Chęciny, Poland

Not demolished. Chęciny's Jewish settlement developed from the end of the 16th century, reaching 2,825 people (56 percent of the town) by 1921, most killed at Treblinka in September 1942. This cemetery, established in the first half of the 17th century and referenced in a royal inventory from 1660 and an 1668 privilege, served as a collective burial ground for several communities, notably Kielce, which itself held the De non tolerandis Judaeis privilege barring Jewish burial there — a fact the historian Majer Bałaban noted in 1929 when observing the cemetery's unusually large size for Chęciny's modest community. From 1942, three people — Guta Szynowłoga, Lilli Szynowłoga, and Izaak Latrowski — hid in the cemetery caretaker's house. About 300 tombstones survive, the oldest dated 1638.
